description: Hi! I'm Yousef, a software engineering student and developer who loves building products that solve real problems. I've led teams in several hackathons and know how to keep a team focused and deliver on time. We're looking for teammates skilled in data, science, design, or presentation, and above all, passionate, reliable people excited to build something meaningful!
summary: Mawsim ("season" in Arabic) lets a smallholder farmer test a crop rotation before planting it. A farmer taps their field anywhere on Earth and answers five plain questions. Mawsim then reads 44 years of daily NASA POWER data for that place and shows what has really changed (rain onset, dry spells, heat, frost), where the climate is heading by 2040 using NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, and which place on Earth lives that future climate today. It runs every candidate rotation through each real season with a daily FAO-56 water balance, so the farmer sees how often a plan would have failed, what it does to soil and water, and what it earns, in their own currency if they enter their own profits. A voice-and-text advisor, Sanad, explains the results in Arabic or English but never invents a number. Most small farms still decide on a calendar the climate has left behind; Mawsim turns NASA's record into a decision a farmer can test before paying for it. It explores options and does not replace the farmer or the extension agent.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mawsim answers four questions for any field on Earth:

1. Field intelligence: What changed on my land? A daily NASA POWER record from 1981 gives seasonal rain, the date of the first effective rain, the longest dry spell, days above 35°C, frost nights and root-zone moisture. Each trend is tested with Mann–Kendall and Theil–Sen so real change is separated from year-to-year noise.

2. Climate twin: Where is my climate heading? Monthly deltas from three NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models (SSP2-4.5, around 2040) are applied to the field's observed climate. A climate-analogue search over 123 farming regions finds the place that lives that climate today and shows what is grown there.

3. Sandbox: What are my options? About 300 candidate rotations are simulated and ranked by what the farmer cares about: profit, safety in bad years, water or soil. Stress tests: drier years, +2°C, a 30% irrigation cut, fertilizer price x2, and the 2040 climate.

4. Time machine: Does the plan hold? Each plan is run through every real season with a daily FAO-56 soil-water balance and FAO yield response. One square per year shows good, fair or poor, and tapping it explains why (late rain, water deficit, heat at flowering, frost, rotation effects).

Example from a real field near Irbid, Jordan: the current wheat–lentil rotation was poor in 8 of 43 seasons; a barley–vetch rotation was poor in 0 of 43 and scored higher on soil health, with similar indicative profit.

AROUND THE FARMER

- My season: the chosen plan becomes a calendar; the sowing window and alerts follow this season's NASA POWER near-real-time observations, not a fixed date. The farm plan prints to PDF.

- Own prices: a farmer can enter their net profit per dunum for each crop in their own currency; every plan is recalculated in it.

- Sanad: an advisor that calls the platform's own tools (change report, twin, plan comparison, new simulation, one season, soil, task, hand-off to an agent) and cites the source. No fertilizer or pesticide doses. Without an API key a local router calls the same tools.

- Extension-agent desk and water-authority portal: farms ranked by risk, plan review, and a policy simulator ("cut the irrigation quota 20%: who is hurt most?"). These run on 28 illustrative farms (invented names, sizes and rotations) over eight real NASA climate cells, and are labelled as such.

- Farmer's library: 16 short practical guides with steps, a tip and a common mistake.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

A rotation is a slow, costly decision whose result shows years later. Mawsim lets a farmer see how a plan would have performed across the 44 seasons their land has already lived through, before paying for seed. It is meant for smallholders, extension services and water planners, starting in the Arab region.

HOW IT IS BUILT

Next.js and TypeScript, Arabic-first and bilingual, usable on a phone. MapLibre GL globe over NASA GIBS imagery. All the science runs as pure functions in the browser (trend statistics, crop-calendar detection, water balance, yield response, rotation ranking, analogue search); about 300 rotations x 44 seasons simulate in roughly half a second. Thin server routes proxy and cache NASA POWER, CMIP6 and SoilGrids. Sanad uses the Claude API. Deployed on Vercel.

CREATIVITY

The climate twin turns an abstract projection into a real place a farmer can relate to. The time machine shows a plan's history season by season instead of one average. Every number has a "Why?" button with its source, period, resolution and confidence.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

- The climate record describes a cell about 50 km wide, not the exact plot.

- Yields, prices and costs are indicative unless the farmer enters their own.

- Pests, varieties, equipment and markets are not modelled.

- The soil-health index is a transparent checklist, not a measurement.

- The tool explores options and does not prescribe; the farmer and the local extension agent decide.
